impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting JMOL that the asserted patent claims directed to humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's grant of JMOL invalidating Teva's headache patents, which cover methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headaches. The jury had found willful infringement and no invalidity, but the district court overturned the verdict. This decision reinstates patent protection for a significant class of migraine therapeutics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain and maintain broad genus claims in the biologics space when the specification discloses known methods for producing claimed antibodies, protecting substantial pharmaceutical revenue streams.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar competitors face continued barriers to entry in the anti-CGRP antibody market, potentially delaying lower-cost alternatives for headache treatments.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who grants an exclusive license but retains meaningful exclusionary rights—including the right to sue third-party infringers—has sufficient Article III standing. The court found the retained right to sue was not illusory given the licensor's retained sublicensing constraints and approval rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring licensing agreements can retain standing to enforce patents even after granting broad exclusive licenses, providing flexibility in monetizing patent portfolios while maintaining enforcement capability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face broader exposure to patent infringement suits from licensors who have licensed away most commercialization rights, potentially complicating settlement negotiations.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in its jury instructions and verdict form by using a single infringement question for multiple patents, and whether the asserted patents directed to wireless building automation systems are invalid under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million patent infringement judgment against ecobee and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's single infringement question covering all asserted patents was prejudicial error. The court also vacated and remanded on the § 101 eligibility analysis for the '495 patent while affirming eligibility for other patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from stricter requirements for verdict forms in multi-patent cases, ensuring juries separately assess infringement for each patent and preventing prejudicial bundling of distinct claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing infringement claims on multiple patents face increased procedural complexity and risk of new trials if verdict forms do not separately address each patent.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether the jury's patent invalidity finding based on inventorship was supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims involving cosmetic penile implant technology, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity and breach of contract but affirmed the counterfeiting verdict and damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses defending against trade secret claims benefit from the court's rigorous application of the requirement that trade secret holders prove information is not generally known, even after a favorable jury verdict.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face a higher evidentiary bar to establish protectability; ideas that are generally known in the field cannot be bootstrapped into trade secret protection even through combination claims.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting two invalidity grounds that were not raised in its original IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding that the court relied on insufficient evidence for one estopped ground and failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in determining that a skilled searcher reasonably could have discovered the prior art for the other ground. The case was remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent litigation benefit from a more rigorous standard for applying IPR estoppel, preserving their ability to raise invalidity defenses that were not included in IPR petitions when the prior art was not reasonably discoverable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders may face expanded invalidity challenges at trial even after prevailing in IPR proceedings, as the scope of estoppel is narrowed.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert testimony and in reducing the jury's breach of contract damages award.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the breach of contract jury award and reinstated the original verdict. Liability for trade secret misappropriation under the DTSA and Michigan law was affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and trade secret holders benefit from broader acceptance of damages models, and the reinstatement of the breach of contract jury award reinforces the sanctity of jury determinations on contract damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop software internally after licensing third-party software face sustained trade secret misappropriation liability, and must carefully manage knowledge barriers when transitioning from licensed to proprietary solutions.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit against EOFlow for misappropriation of insulin pump trade secrets.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict and damages judgment in favor of Insulet, holding that EOFlow was entitled to JMOL because the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing, based on publicly available information about the EOPatch 2 and the former employees' involvement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's statute of limitations, providing a firm cutoff against stale claims even where the plaintiff eventually obtains strong evidence of misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover potential misappropriation; delayed investigation or litigation strategy can result in complete loss of DTSA claims.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate deposition witness may testify to matters outside personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar of 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge and that computer source code is not hearsay because it constitutes machine commands rather than human assertions. The court found sufficient evidence that a prior art device was sold more than one year before the patent's priority date.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity benefit from the ruling that 30(b)(6) witnesses can testify beyond personal knowledge and that source code is admissible as non-hearsay, making it easier to prove on-sale bar and prior art defenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to invalidity challenges based on historical product sales, as corporations can designate witnesses to testify about events predating their tenure, and source code evidence is more readily admissible.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the definition of a substituent between a provisional and non-provisional patent application constituted an obvious typographical error correctable without adding new matter, thereby preserving the earlier priority date.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that Enanta's '953 patent was invalid as anticipated by Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid). The court held that the change from C2 to C1 in the alkyl range was not an obvious typographical error, so the patent could not claim priority from the earlier provisional application, making Pfizer's public disclosure prior art.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical companies like Pfizer benefit from clear rules on priority claims, ensuring that competitors cannot retroactively correct patent specifications to capture priority dates that predate intervening disclosures.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent applicants face severe consequences for even minor drafting errors in provisional applications; a single character difference can result in loss of priority and complete patent invalidation.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of doctrine of equivalents theories for patents relating to multi-core processor task allocation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially reversed summary judgment of noninfringement in VLSI's patent case against Intel concerning multi-core processor technology. The court reversed the extraterritoriality ruling while affirming the rejection of certain doctrine of equivalents theories, and also reversed the striking of damages expert theories, remanding for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of semiconductor and processor technology patents benefit from the court's narrowing of the extraterritoriality defense, potentially expanding the scope of domestic patent enforcement for globally manufactured chips.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor companies and other technology firms with multinational manufacturing operations face broader patent infringement exposure for products with design and testing steps occurring partly in the United States.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in not finding the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's patent claims for automated farming data collection were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorney fees under § 285. The court found the claims merely automated conventional data collection practices.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in agricultural technology patent cases benefit from continued rigorous application of § 101 to data collection and processing claims, and the remand on exceptionality signals the court's willingness to award fees against weak patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech companies and patent holders face significant hurdles in patenting automated data collection systems, as claims that automate conventional practices without inventive technological improvements are likely ineligible.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility, finding that certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents required further analysis under Alice, while affirming eligibility for other patents. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, upholding a jury verdict of willful infringement against LG for its television products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the digital communications space benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for patents implementing specific technical improvements in signal constellation design, and the damages and infringement holdings support enforcement of standards-related patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing industry standards face infringement liability for standards-essential patent claims that survive § 101 challenges, potentially increasing licensing costs for consumer electronics.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner may correct inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) through court proceedings when a co-inventor cannot be located, and whether failure to include a known co-inventor renders the patent invalid.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of patent invalidity due to omission of a co-inventor (a Chinese manufacturer's employee) who could not be located. The court upheld the denial of Fortress's motion to judicially correct inventorship under § 256(b), finding that the inability to locate the omitted inventor did not excuse the inventorship defect.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from strict enforcement of inventorship requirements, providing a powerful invalidity defense when patent owners fail to properly name all inventors, particularly in collaborative international development arrangements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that collaborate with foreign manufacturers on product development face significant patent vulnerability if foreign contributors to the invention cannot later be located for inventorship correction, potentially invalidating valuable patents.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination when an IPR petition was filed by an entity that was not a party to the underlying patent infringement litigation but filed on the deadline applicable to the defendant in that litigation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness finding invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. While declining to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR, the court found errors in the Board's obviousness analysis. The case highlights concerns about third-party IPR petitions filed to benefit litigation defendants.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from closer scrutiny of PTAB obviousness determinations and may gain protection against strategically timed third-party IPR petitions that appear coordinated with litigation defendants.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge patent validity through IPR face greater uncertainty about the Board's analysis surviving appellate review, potentially increasing the cost and risk of IPR proceedings.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents should be measured at a standard temperature (25°C) or at the temperature of reconstitution, and whether the doctrine of equivalents was properly barred.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents by Mylan's generic drug, holding that the pH claim limitation must be measured at the standard temperature convention in the field (25°C). The court also affirmed that Actelion was barred from asserting infringement by equivalents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from clear guidance that pH claim limitations are interpreted under standard measurement conventions, providing certainty for ANDA filers designing around branded drug patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies face narrower claim scope when patent claims reference measurable physical parameters, as courts will apply standard measurement conditions rather than conditions that might capture a broader range of competing products.
